```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  prompt = FALSE,
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4.5,
  out.width = "100%"
)
source_roots <- c(".", "..")
source_roots <- source_roots[
  file.exists(file.path(source_roots, "DESCRIPTION"))
]
if (length(source_roots) && requireNamespace("pkgload", quietly = TRUE)) {
  pkgload::load_all(
    source_roots[[1L]],
    quiet = TRUE,
    export_all = FALSE
  )
} else {
  library(readPBOC)
}

live_examples <- identical(
  Sys.getenv("READPBOC_LIVE_EXAMPLES"),
  "true"
)

package_file <- function(...) {
  pieces <- c(...)
  relative <- do.call(file.path, as.list(pieces))
  candidates <- c(
    file.path(source_roots, "inst", relative),
    system.file(..., package = "readPBOC")
  )
  found <- candidates[
    nzchar(candidates) & file.exists(candidates) & !dir.exists(candidates)
  ]
  if (!length(found)) {
    stop(
      "Could not find the packaged example file ",
      paste(pieces, collapse = "/"),
      ". Build or install readPBOC before rendering this vignette."
    )
  }
  normalizePath(found[[1L]], winslash = "/", mustWork = TRUE)
}

money_cells <- utils::read.csv(
  package_file("extdata", "readpboc-worksheet-fixture.csv"),
  header = FALSE,
  check.names = FALSE,
  na.strings = "",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  fileEncoding = "UTF-8"
)

money_snapshot_file <- package_file(
  "examples", "data", "pboc-current-series-values.rds"
)
```

## A complete path from source to analysis

`readPBOC` follows a PBOC data workflow from discovery to an auditable local
file. The package has four layers:

1. `pboc_years()`,
   `pboc_sections()`,
   and `pboc_catalog()`
   discover the Chinese and English archives.
2. `pboc_read()`
   reads a local or remote spreadsheet/HTML table, while
   `pboc_tidy()`
   turns irregular worksheet cells into long observations.
3. `pboc_releases()`
   and `pboc_read_release()`
   index and read statistical statements.
4. `pboc_download()`,
   `pboc_snapshot()`,
   and `pboc_revisions()`
   preserve source files and make catalog changes explicit.

PBOC pages and attachments are public, so these workflows require no account
or API key. The examples combine a small author-created parser fixture with a
provenance-recorded PBOC snapshot, allowing the complete article to render
offline while retaining a clear path to the live source.

## Installation

The development version can be installed from GitHub:

```{r install, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("chartwell-macro/readPBoC")
```

After a release is accepted by CRAN, the stable installation route will be:

```{r cran-install, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("readPBOC")
```

Until then, GitHub is the current installation source.

## Know what the example covers

The live Chinese and English archives are independent inventories, not paired
translations. A listed year does not guarantee that the same table, period,
format, or publication date exists in both languages. The packaged numeric
snapshot used below is Chinese-source data with bilingual labels: it contains
26 current-year workbooks and 3,095 observations, mostly from January through
June 2026. Financial-market tables currently end in May, one overseas-assets
table ends in March, and the reserves/liquidity template is a 30 June
point-in-time table.

Missing rows are not zeros. The packaged snapshot includes sparse pledged-repo
trading-volume series, while its Money and Money & Quasi-money series each
contain all six months from January through June. See
[Discovering and reading data](discovering-and-reading-data.html#understand-coverage-before-reading)
for the complete packaged-coverage summary, language differences, and a gap
check that can be reused for other series.

## Retrieve and chart a time series

The explicit online path is discovery, selection, and reading. The following
opt-in chunk narrows the 2026 Chinese catalog to the Money Supply workbook,
requires one unambiguous match, and passes that row to `pboc_read()` with
normalisation enabled:

```{r retrieve-money-supply-live, eval=live_examples}
money_catalog <- pboc_catalog(
  2026,
  language = "zh",
  section = "money_and_banking",
  formats = "xlsx"
)
money_asset <- money_catalog[
  grepl("Money Supply|货币供应量", money_catalog$item),
  ,
  drop = FALSE
]
stopifnot(nrow(money_asset) == 1L)
money_supply <- pboc_read(
  money_asset[1L, , drop = FALSE],
  sheet = 1,
  tidy = TRUE
)
```

Set `READPBOC_LIVE_EXAMPLES=true` to run that live path deliberately. The
default vignette build uses the installed normalised snapshot for the same
attachment revision (`2026071516481518348`), published on 15 July 2026. This
keeps documentation and CRAN builds deterministic while preserving the
official URL, raw values, units, and worksheet coordinates.

```{r load-money-supply-snapshot, include=FALSE}
if (!exists("money_supply", inherits = FALSE)) {
  money_values <- readRDS(money_snapshot_file)
  money_supply <- money_values[
    money_values$revision_id == "2026071516481518348",
    ,
    drop = FALSE
  ]
}
```

The source unit is RMB 100 million, so divide `value` by 10,000 to express the
levels in RMB trillion. No additional reshaping package is needed:

```{r prepare-money-supply-chart}
chart_data <- money_supply[
  money_supply$series %in% c("Money", "Money & Quasi-money") &
    !is.na(money_supply$value),
  c("series", "period", "value"),
  drop = FALSE
]
chart_data$date <- as.Date(
  paste0(sub("\\.", "-", chart_data$period), "-01")
)
chart_data$value <- chart_data$value / 10000
chart_data <- chart_data[order(chart_data$series, chart_data$date), ]
head(chart_data)
```

```{r validate-money-supply-chart, include=FALSE}
stopifnot(
  nrow(chart_data) > 0L,
  !anyNA(chart_data[c("series", "date", "value")])
)
if (!live_examples) {
  stopifnot(nrow(chart_data) == 12L)
}
```

```{r money-supply-chart, fig.alt="Line chart of PBOC M1 and M2 money-supply levels from January to June 2026, in RMB trillion."}
if (requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)) {
  ggplot2::ggplot(
    chart_data,
    ggplot2::aes(x = date, y = value, colour = series, group = series)
  ) +
    ggplot2::geom_line() +
    ggplot2::labs(
      title = "PBOC money supply",
      subtitle = "Monthly published observations",
      x = "Month",
      y = "RMB trillion",
      colour = "Series",
      caption = "Source: People's Bank of China website"
    ) +
    ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
}
```

Required source attribution: 稿件来源：中国人民银行网站 (Source: People's Bank
of China website).

The chart uses the public output columns returned by both paths: `series`,
canonical monthly `period`, and numeric `value`. The README homepage shows the
shorter one-call `pboc_data()` equivalent.

## Read and normalise a local worksheet

The packaged structural fixture is a small, author-created worksheet-shaped
CSV. It is read as character cells and passed to `pboc_tidy()`, which detects
dated headers, keeps bilingual labels where present, and retains source
coordinates. Its synthetic values provide a compact parser demonstration.

```{r first-success}
money <- pboc_tidy(money_cells)
stopifnot(is.data.frame(money), all(c("period", "value") %in% names(money)))

names(money)
head(money[c("series", "period", "value", "value_raw")])
```

The result is a tibble with a stable audit-oriented shape. The main columns are
`table`, `series`, `series_zh`, `series_en`, `period`, `value`, `value_raw`,
`unit`, `source_row`, and `source_column`. `value` is numeric when it can be
parsed; `value_raw` retains the source text. Periods are normalised to labels
such as `2025.01`, while source row and column numbers point back to the
original worksheet. Any notes detected below the table are stored in the
`"notes"` attribute.

```{r inspect-contract}
class(money)
attributes(money)[intersect(
  c("notes", "source_url", "source_path"),
  names(attributes(money))
)]
```

This is the useful boundary for downstream code: select a series, filter a
period, and use `value` for calculations while keeping `value_raw` and source
coordinates for review. Persistent storage remains an explicit caller choice.

## Continue with live data and provenance

* To locate a current workbook, start with
  `pboc_catalog()`
  and then pass one catalog row to `pboc_read()` or `pboc_data()`.
* To read an already downloaded workbook or HTML table, use
  `pboc_read()`.
* To preserve a release and compare future catalogs, see
  `pboc_download()`
  and
  `pboc_revisions()`.
* For request limits, storage behaviour, and recovery guidance, read the
  [Network, authentication, and troubleshooting](network-authentication-troubleshooting.html)
  article.

## Scope and limitations

`readPBOC` normalises XLS/XLSX workbooks and exposes HTML tables. It catalogs
and preserves PDFs for use with a dedicated PDF tool. Live discovery depends
on the official site's availability and markup, while packaged snapshots are
frozen evidence rather than a current-data service. Retain source URLs,
revision identifiers, and manifests when a result must be reproduced.
